research_domain_title: Community Resource Compacts, Progressive Resource Pricing, Local Dividends, and Ecological Restoration
note: Central developing doctrine. Community Resource Compacts, Local Carbon Restoration Exchange, and Resource and Pollution Ledger are design agendas — not operating products. Illustrative revenue percentages require modeling. No invented water, electricity, emission, or carbon-credit statistics. Detailed statutes blocked until Phase 2.1 sourced modules. Federal GHGRP rules are politically changeable and must not be treated as a permanent floor.
role_in_philosophy: Land, water, minerals, energy capacity, clean air, soil, infrastructure, and ecological resilience are part of a community’s inherited wealth. Private enterprise may profit from using those resources, but the affected community must receive a direct, permanent, and measurable return. This connects environmental protection, local ownership, household affordability, rural prosperity, regenerative agriculture, energy resilience, and corporate accountability.

central_doctrine.text: Natural resources belong first to the place that bears the extraction, consumption, congestion, pollution, and long-term risk. Private enterprise may profit from using those resources, but the affected community must receive a direct, permanent, and measurable return.

governing_statement.text: Land, water, minerals, energy capacity, clean air, soil, infrastructure, and ecological resilience are part of a community’s inherited wealth. Those who consume them for private gain must pay their full public cost, restore what they damage, and return a fair share of the resulting prosperity to the people and place that made the activity possible.

operational_rule.text: The greater the consumption, scarcity, risk, or damage, the greater the obligation to the affected community.

not_free_inputs.text: The system should not treat water, minerals, land, grid capacity, clean air, roads, and soil as free inputs merely because a corporation can obtain a permit.

community_resource_compact.summary: Every large resource-consuming project would negotiate a binding Community Resource Compact before receiving public approval, incentives, utility commitments, or infrastructure access.
applies_especially_to: large developments consuming farmland or habitat
facilities creating substantial truck traffic, emissions, waste, or grid demand
determines: What resources will the project consume?
What burdens and risks will the community absorb?
What direct benefits will remain in the community?
What restoration obligations continue after the project closes?

progressive_resource_pricing.summary: Consumption should not be priced as a flat fee. A small business, family farm, or household should not pay the same marginal rate as a billion-dollar facility consuming extraordinary quantities of water, electricity, land, or road capacity.

tiers.title: Commercial-use tier
for: normal business activity using resources within ordinary local capacity

tiers.title: Intensive-use tier
for: projects consuming substantially above community norms

tiers.title: Transformative-use tier
for: projects whose consumption changes the community’s infrastructure, environment, utility planning, water table, grid demand, traffic, or land use

progressive_resource_pricing.conceptual_formula: Base resource price + volume surcharge + scarcity surcharge + environmental-risk charge + infrastructure charge + restoration bond.
progressive_resource_pricing.purpose: Not merely to collect money — to ensure the business decision includes the real public cost of the project.
progressive_resource_pricing.pricing_principle: Essential human use receives protection. Extraordinary commercial use pays its full marginal and community cost.

total_footprint_assessment.summary: Charge for the total footprint, not only the resource removed. A lithium operation does not affect only the mineral deposit; a data center does not affect only the electricity meter; a warehouse does not affect only the parcel of land.
total_footprint_assessment.scope_1_scope_2_rule: Major projects must disclose and price both direct emissions controlled by a facility and indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity, rather than appearing clean simply because emissions occur at a distant power plant.

community_resource_dividend.summary: A large share of every resource charge should remain where the impact occurs, divided into protected accounts.

accounts.title: Future Generations Fund
accounts.summary: A permanent fund should convert temporary extraction into lasting community wealth so future residents continue receiving benefits after the resource is gone.

illustrative_allocation.note: Percentages are conceptual starters, not locked policy.

community_resource_dividend.firm_doctrine: The majority of geographically concentrated impact revenue must return to the affected place.

community_equity.summary: Fees can be negotiated away or spent quickly. For exceptionally large projects, the community should receive a continuing ownership interest so it becomes a participant in the project’s success rather than a location rented for extraction.
possible_structures: shares held by a local public trust
appreciation rights if the facility is sold

mineral_extraction_compact.summary: Critical minerals are strategically important, but strategic importance should not erase local rights.
mineral_extraction_compact.federal_context_note: Interior Department materials recognize the need for mining systems that provide reliable mineral supplies while addressing environmental and social responsibility, Tribal interests, climate risks, and modern standards.
requirements: community and Tribal consultation before final siting
independent air, soil, and groundwater monitoring
local processing where economically and environmentally responsible
reclamation bonding sufficient for worst-case closure
public disclosure of ownership and mineral sales
mineral_extraction_compact.rate_rule: The rate should increase as extraction grows or as the resource becomes scarcer.
mineral_extraction_compact.bankruptcy_rule: A company should never be able to extract the valuable resource, declare bankruptcy, and leave the public with the cleanup.

data_center_compact.summary: Data centers require a distinct framework because they may create enormous electricity, water, land, and backup-generation demands while employing relatively few people after construction.
data_center_compact.federal_context_note: EPA provides Clean Air Act-related resources concerning data-center power sources and backup generation, reflecting air-quality and permitting implications of those facilities.
should_pay: the full cost of dedicated infrastructure
data_center_compact.residential_protection_rule: Residential customers should never subsidize the infrastructure or electricity discounts of an extraordinary corporate user.
data_center_compact.generation_addition_rule: A new data center should demonstrate that it adds generation or efficiency sufficient to prevent residential rates from rising because of its arrival.

warehouse_compact.summary: Large warehouses may create more jobs than data centers, but can also produce heavy truck traffic, road damage, diesel pollution, land consumption, housing/service pressure, and automation-related displacement. The community must receive more than temporary construction jobs and traffic.
requirements: road-use assessments based on vehicle weight and volume
wage and benefit standards where public incentives are involved

resource_and_pollution_ledger.summary: Price more than carbon. Large facilities already report certain facility-level greenhouse-gas information through EPA’s reporting framework, although federal reporting rules are politically changeable. Constitutional Capitalism should establish a durable public Resource and Pollution Ledger.
progressive_charges: punitive for concealed, unlawful, or repeated releases

local_carbon_restoration_exchange.summary: High-carbon and high-resource users should finance locally verified carbon removal and ecological restoration. Create a public or cooperative exchange at the county or regional level. High-emitting entities pay in; local farmers, foresters, landowners, and restoration groups compete for contracts.
local_carbon_restoration_exchange.federal_context_note: USDA/NRCS recognizes climate-smart mitigation and soil-management practices as potential tools with co-benefits for soil health, water quality, erosion, and habitat. USDA has also launched soil-carbon measurement and monitoring efforts, underscoring why credible measurement must be central.

anti_fraud_carbon_hierarchy.summary: A company should not be allowed to continue unlimited pollution simply because it purchased inexpensive credits with questionable value. Local carbon removal should supplement — not excuse — emissions reduction.
hierarchy: Offset only the genuinely difficult remainder

community_owned_energy.summary: Every community should be encouraged to produce a meaningful share of the electricity it consumes. The goal is not total isolation from the regional grid, but local price stability, resilience, emergency power, reduced transmission loss, community ownership, income retained locally, and less vulnerability to large industrial loads.
community_owned_energy.community_solar_note: DOE defines community solar as a geographically based project or purchasing program whose benefits flow to multiple customers such as individuals, businesses, nonprofits, and other groups.

household_energy_floor.summary: Every household should receive a protected block of essential electricity at the lowest sustainable price covering basic lighting, refrigeration, heating or cooling, cooking, communication, and medical devices. Usage beyond the protected household level could rise gradually. Large industrial consumption would face a steeper curve unless the company adds new generation, storage, or efficiency.

community_carrying_capacity_test.title: Community Carrying-Capacity Test
community_carrying_capacity_test.purpose: Screen every major facility before approval.

questions.text: How much water will it use?
How much power will it require?
What portion of local grid capacity will it consume?
What land will be permanently changed?
What roads and public systems will it burden?
What lasting jobs and ownership will it create?
Will households pay higher prices because of it?
What happens when the facility closes?
What permanent wealth remains in the community?
Can the community reject or renegotiate the project?
Is the project still beneficial after all public costs are counted?

research_status.next: Phase 2.1: deepen EPA/USDA/DOE/DOI modules; model dividend allocations without locking illustrative percentages; attach baseline indicators; keep Compacts/Exchange/Ledger as design agendas
